items.content:
"Three out of four are defective"... China's CXMT struggles with HBM yields, with immature TSV technology to blame

ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT), China's largest DRAM maker, has begun trial production of fourth generation high bandwidth memory (HBM3), but initial yields are barely improving. Yields are reported to have stalled at 25%, roughly one third of the so called "golden yield" of 80% that the semiconductor industry treats as the threshold for volume production. The gap is stark compared with SK hynix, which has been mass producing the same product since 2022 and has secured yields above 90%. Industry sources point to the gap in maturity of through-silicon via (TSV) technology, the core process for stacking and connecting multiple DRAM layers, as the root cause.

◇ "DRAM has caught up, but HBM stacking is a different problem"

According to a senior official at a semiconductor equipment company familiar with CXMT's situation on the 9th, the yield of CXMT's HBM3 8-High product is stuck at around 30% in the front end process. Of the products that survive that stage, only about 70% are recognized as final good units after passing through the back end process. In simple terms, if 100 HBM3 units are started, close to 80 of them fail the final test.

CXMT is reported to be supplying the small volumes of HBM samples it produces this way to Chinese companies such as Alibaba's T-Head and Cambricon while continuing its yield improvement work. The problem is that the issue does not lie in the fine process technology of the DRAM itself. A semiconductor equipment industry official explained, "There is no major problem with the standard DRAM that CXMT makes on its 'G4' (17nm class) process used for HBM. However, the DRAM dies used for HBM are larger in area than standard products and have more demanding electrical specifications, so even on the same process they are much harder to pass the acceptance criteria."

In other words, CXMT's fundamental capability in making standard DRAM has risen to a considerable level, but a bottleneck is emerging at the stage of converting it into the high performance product that is HBM. At the heart of that bottleneck, according to industry sources, is the TSV process.

◇ The real hurdle is TSV... "Impossible to catch up without years of accumulated know how"

TSV stands for "Through Silicon Via" and refers to the microscopic copper wiring that passes vertically through each layer to carry electrical signals when DRAM is stacked in multiple layers, as in HBM. It is a highly demanding process in which a DRAM wafer is thinned down to several tens of micrometers, a fraction of the thickness of a human hair, after which thousands of tiny holes are drilled through that thin silicon plate and filled completely with copper. A single hole that is misaligned or not properly filled can cause the entire layer to be rejected, making it one of the semiconductor processes with the most stringent precision requirements.

The consensus in the industry is that this is the process where the technology gap between CXMT and the leading companies is widest. According to analysis by semiconductor research firm Nomad Semi, Samsung Electronics' HBM2 (second generation HBM) has more than 5,000 TSVs per die and SK hynix's HBM3 has more than 8,000, while CXMT's is understood to have only around 3,000. A smaller number of TSVs means sacrificing bandwidth (data processing speed) in exchange for lower process difficulty, yet even so CXMT's yields still fall far short of Samsung and SK hynix. TSV is a process that is challenging even for the industry leader: SK hynix itself publicly disclosed in 2024 that the yield of the standalone TSV process was only 40 to 60% at the time.

On top of this, yield losses also occur in the back end (stacking and bonding) stage where the dies are actually stacked and joined. If even one of the eight dies is misaligned, if a microscopic void forms at a bonding interface, or if a layer warps during the thermocompression bonding process (warpage), the entire stack is scrapped. Because the number of possible failure points grows with each additional layer, the difficulty rises exponentially. Given that CXMT is already showing such poor yields at 8-High, some expect it to face even greater difficulties when moving to higher stacks such as 12-High.

A semiconductor industry official explained, "The TSV process is an area that only stabilizes after years of accumulated wafer handling know how. Chinese companies have rapidly closed the gap in the fine process technology of DRAM itself, but back end know how such as TSV and bonding is difficult to catch up on in a short period." He added, "That said, Samsung Electronics also had initial HBM4 (sixth generation HBM) production yields below 60% in February this year and raised them to 80% within six months, so it is too early to declare CXMT's 25% yield a 'failure.'"
— Jukan (@jukan05) Sep 8, 2026

items.content:
Samsung Display Sharply Raises Next Year's Supply Targets for Apple Foldable and iPad OLED

Samsung Display has reportedly set a business plan to significantly expand next year's supply volume, centered on foldable phones and iPads, Apple's new OLED demand sources. The company is targeting 15 million foldable OLED panels next year, up from around 8 million this year, and 9 million iPad OLED panels, up from around 2 million this year. Combined OLED supply for Apple foldables and tablets would more than double, from a total of 10 million units this year to roughly 24 million. According to industry sources on the 8th, Samsung Display plans to substantially expand its shipments of foldable and tablet OLED for Apple next year.

Apple is the key customer of Samsung Display's small and mid sized OLED business. It typically supplies more than 100 million OLED panels a year for the iPhone series alone. According to market research firm UBI Research, total demand for iPhone OLED panels this year is 264.7 million units, of which Samsung Display is expected to supply 144 million. Samsung Display is understood to be planning a similar volume next year. The target currently set is around 148 million units. While iPhone OLED panels are expected to stagnate, supply growth next year is anticipated to come from new demand sources. The representative product is foldable OLED. Apple will launch its first foldable phone in the second half of this year.

Accordingly, Samsung Display plans to expand shipments of its 7.8 inch foldable OLED panels for Apple from 8 million this year to around 15 million next year, nearly double. The figure reflects volumes for this year's first model and a new model to be launched next year. For tablet OLED panels, the company is targeting around 9 million next year, up from around 2 million this year. After adopting OLED in two iPad Pro models (11 and 13 inch) in 2024, Apple decided to adopt OLED in the iPad mini (8.5 inch) this year as well. Next year, it will extend adoption to two iPad Air models (11 and 13 inch). However, Samsung Display's supply targets could change at any time depending on market conditions going forward. The key variables are Apple's pricing policy in response to the surge in memory prices and the resulting swings in IT demand.

For foldable phones, there is also uncertainty on the supply chain side. Concerns are widespread in the industry that shipments of Apple's foldable phone will fall short of expectations this year due to yield problems with core components such as the hinge and substrate. A display industry official explained, "Assuming Apple's foldable phone launches at around $2,500 (approximately 3.36 million won), shipments of roughly 6 million and 11 million units would be possible this year and next year, respectively. If the price is higher than that or supply chain issues intensify, shipments could fall further."

items.content:
Samsung Foundry Launches Its Counterattack: "Full Capacity" Before Full Operation Even Begins

Samsung Electronics' foundry division is mounting a major counteroffensive in the global foundry market dominated by Taiwan's TSMC, riding on large orders from US big tech companies such as Tesla and Broadcom. The Taylor foundry fab in Texas, which is set to begin pilot operation as early as the end of this month, has already reached "full capacity" with its planned production volume fully booked, and it has been confirmed that the company is also pushing ahead with the introduction of equipment from domestic suppliers for the second fab, which breaks ground at the end of the year.

The move is seen as a decisive bet to secure mass production capabilities on par with TSMC in the 2nm node, the cutting edge process that will determine leadership in the global foundry market next year, and to capture big tech's demand to move away from TSMC.

According to the semiconductor industry on the 8th, Samsung's Taylor fab in the US has effectively reached full capacity before even starting operation, as 2nm orders keep coming in, including Tesla's next generation AI chip "AI5," Broadcom's next generation communications chip, and an AI chip for smart devices from the UK's Arm. The 2nm yield , which stood at around 60% earlier this year, is reported to have recently reached the 80% range, a level that makes mass production possible, helped by the stabilization of yields on existing advanced nodes such as 4nm and 5nm.

The Taylor fab, which Samsung has built since 2022 with an investment of $37 billion (about 52 trillion won), will go through pilot operation early next month and begin volume production next year. Its initial production capacity is 50,000 wafer inputs per month, close to the level of Taiwan's TSMC (80,000). Samsung previously dispatched process, equipment, and yield personnel to the Taylor fab in June and began equipment installation in July.

With the Taylor fab, the core base of Samsung Foundry, entering full capacity, the earnings of the foundry business, long the "sore spot" of the Device Solutions (DS) division, are also rising quickly. At its recent earnings call, Samsung projected that its 2nm order volume this year would more than double from last year. Nvidia's inference only chip "Groq 3" also entered mass production last month. Built on the 4nm process, Groq 3 is a rack scale system that bundles 256 language processing units (LPUs) and is tasked with expanding the inference performance of the next generation AI platform "Vera Rubin." Samsung's recent price increase of up to 15% on its 4nm foundry services has also contributed to the improvement in earnings.

Preparations for the second Taylor fab, which breaks ground at the end of this year with mass production targeted for 2030, are also accelerating. Samsung is reported to have recently asked major suppliers to obtain safety certification in advance for the chip production equipment to be installed in the second fab. Some suppliers are also said to be pushing plans to dispatch dozens of personnel on site for the construction of the second Taylor fab.

The back and forth battle for leadership is heating up as well. In the US, Intel issued $20 billion in new shares last month and is expanding investment in its 2nm class "18A" process and next generation 1.4nm class "14A." Rapidus, the symbol of Japan's semiconductor revival, also completed its 2nm foundry fab in Hokkaido last month and has entered the pilot wafer input stage.
— Jukan (@jukan05) Sep 8, 2026

items.content:
DIGITIMES' latest report on Intel:

Intel will raise prices on PC CPUs by another 10% in October.

At the same time, the Small Core product line, which carries lower gross margins, may be headed toward EOL (End of Life).

This would open an opportunity for Qualcomm and MediaTek from the ARM camp to enter the industrial PC (IPC) and Internet of Things (IoT) chip markets.

There is also talk that Intel will cut a further 5% to 10% of its workforce.

In July, Intel carried out another round of layoffs targeting its Data Center and AI (DCAI) group, and its global headcount is currently estimated at roughly 75,000.

However, sources cited by DIGITIMES noted that Intel will be hiring new staff alongside the cuts, and that the current organization, already trimmed to just over 70,000 employees, is already fairly reasonable in size.

According to the industry, global PC shipments will reach roughly 260 million units in 2026, but may decline slightly to about 250 million units in 2027.

The main cause is not a sharp contraction in PC demand, but rather that recent steep increases in the prices of components such as memory and PCBs have begun to pile cost pressure onto finished systems.

Industry sources said that in response to the broad surge in costs, Intel has been raising PC CPU prices in stages over the past year, and tentatively plans another 10% increase in early October. The fact that Intel has chosen to raise CPU prices even as the finished PC market is expected to shrink slightly in 2027 shows that its top priority is improving gross margin rather than expanding market share.

With the global PC market holding at roughly 250 million units, DIGITIMES assessed that if Intel can bring its CPU shipments back up to nearly 200 million units, its market share could recover to about 78%. At the same time, lifting ASP through price adjustments should help restore profitability in its PC CPU business.

DIGITIMES also reported that Intel currently faces a tougher problem in server CPUs than in PC CPUs. According to the supply chain, Intel is currently prioritizing its own fab capacity for server CPUs. The gross margin on server CPUs it manufactures in house is higher than on products outsourced to TSMC, but server CPU capacity still cannot keep up with demand, and this is crowding out PC CPU capacity as well.

DIGITIMES assessed that if Intel wants to further accelerate the expansion of server CPU production, it may have to hand part of the volume to TSMC, and that this is the manufacturing dilemma Intel currently faces. This is why the yield of the 18A process and the development progress of the 14A process are drawing attention.

Samsung Adopts the Same Silicon Photonics Development Partners as TSMC

Samsung Electronics has been found to have selected the same development partners as Taiwan's TSMC for silicon photonics, a technology that uses light to reduce semiconductor bottlenecks, heat, and power consumption. On this basis, the company plans to complete wafer testing of photonic integrated circuits (PICs) for silicon photonics within the year.

According to industry sources on the 7th, Samsung Electronics is testing PIC wafers for silicon photonics using probe stations from FormFactor of the United States and MPI of Taiwan, both test interface companies. Optical and electrical measurement equipment is linked to the probe stations to measure the wavelength domain and the frequency domain. The key is to verify that the optical devices implemented on the wafer transmit light as designed and convert between electrical and optical signals.

A probe station is a piece of equipment used to measure the characteristics of semiconductor devices. It holds a wafer or an individual die in place and brings probes that carry electrical signals into contact with the electrodes, connecting them to external measurement equipment. Probe stations for silicon photonics add the capability to precisely align optical fibers with the optical input and output ports of the PIC. Once the measurement equipment injects optical and electrical signals and measures the output, the probe station moves the wafer to repeat the inspection on the next die.

An industry source said, "Samsung Electronics is evaluating PIC wafers in house with the goal of completing the work within the year," adding that "it is using the two probe station vendors that passed TSMC's equipment qualification for CPO and silicon photonics testing." In effect, Samsung is verifying its PICs with the same test infrastructure used by the industry leader.

TSMC uses probe stations from FormFactor and MPI for the development and verification of COUPE (Co-Packaged Optical Engine), its silicon photonics based CPO platform. To date, these are the only two companies that have passed TSMC's qualification for CPO related test equipment.

Since last year, Samsung Electronics has had its PIC wafers verified by outside parties such as imec, the Belgian semiconductor research institute. It has now built its own test environment and is conducting repeated evaluations. This is an optimization stage in which the company evaluates the performance of PIC wafers based on initial designs and feeds the measurement results back into the design.

Preparations for customer evaluations are also under way in parallel. Global networking and communications chip companies such as Broadcom are being mentioned as prospective customers. In its first quarter earnings release this year, Samsung Electronics announced that it had won a project from a major optical communications module company, securing a foundation for its silicon photonics business. It said it would begin mass production for the project in the second half of the year.

A PIC integrates optical devices such as waveguides, through which light travels; modulators, which convert electrical signals into optical signals by loading them onto light; and photodetectors, which convert optical signals back into electrical signals. Samsung Electronics measures wavelength domain and frequency domain characteristics to optimize optical loss, response by wavelength, and bandwidth.

After PIC testing, the company plans to expand the scope of testing to optical engines that combine an electronic integrated circuit (EIC) with the PIC. The EIC is a chip that processes and amplifies electrical signals to drive the optical devices on the PIC. The EIC and PIC are stacked and combined with the optical path that connects to external optical fibers to form a single optical engine. Optical engine testing is expected to add time domain measurements to verify actual high speed data transmission performance.

Samsung Electronics will launch its silicon photonics foundry service in 2027. It will provide process technology for implementing optical devices, an optical device library, and a process design kit (PDK). Customers will use these to design PICs, which Samsung Foundry will then manufacture in wafer form. Development of the optical engine combining the EIC and PIC will begin this year, with testing to start next year.

The ultimate plan is to package the optical engine together with logic and high bandwidth memory (HBM). In a mockup unveiled recently, Samsung Electronics showed a structure in which a logic chip and an optical engine are placed together on a silicon interposer. Inside the optical engine, the PIC and EIC are stacked in three dimensions (3D) using methods such as hybrid bonding to shorten the connection distance. Going forward, the company plans to expand the scope of CPO from network switches to GPUs and CPUs.

Choi Won kyoung, Vice President of the Advanced Package Lab at Samsung Electronics' Semiconductor R&D Center, said at Nano Korea in July, "We are currently developing optical devices such as PICs ourselves," adding, "We plan to focus on developing an optical engine that integrates the EIC, PIC, and optical connection into one, enter the silicon photonics market, and then expand the application to switch, GPU, and CPU products."
— Jukan (@jukan05) Sep 7, 2026
